title: Big-O intuition (read complexity off code shapes)
description: Read time complexity off the code shape — what loop and recursion structures map to O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n log n), and O(n²). Meta-lesson: the canonical is a recognition checklist, not one algorithm.

conversation.intro: How you'd justify a Big-O claim in an interview — not 'recite the answer' but 'derive it out loud from the code shape'. Each section: what you'd say, then why that move matters.

sections.title: 1. Why drill this?
sections.prompt: Every interview ends with 'what's the complexity?' — be ready.
sections.say:
"Every algorithm question I've had ends with the interviewer asking 'and what's the time and space complexity?'. They're not testing whether I memorized the answer for THIS problem — they're testing whether I can READ a piece of code and derive O(...) from its shape. So this is the recognition skill: see a single loop → O(n); see a halving loop → O(log n); see two nested loops over the same input → O(n²); see a sort followed by anything → O(n log n) until something blows past it."

"My script for any complexity question is the same: name the shape, count the work per element, multiply, then add the secondary costs and drop them if they're smaller."
sections.why: Frame the lesson as a *technique* (read-off-the-shape) rather than memorization. Interviewers can tell when a candidate has memorized 'two-sum is O(n)' vs when they can defend any algorithm's complexity by pointing at the lines. The recognition-from-shape skill is the transferable one — it works on problems you haven't seen before.

sections.title: 2. The common mistakes first
sections.prompt: What goes wrong in candidate complexity answers?
sections.say:
"Three failure modes I'd guard against:"

• "Calling nested loops O(n²) without checking whether the inner is bounded by n. `for j in 0..k` with k a constant gives O(n·k) = O(n), not O(n²). The inner has to depend on n for the outer multiplication to compound."

• "Confusing O(n log n) for any sort — quicksort's WORST case is O(n²), and counting sort / radix sort can do O(n) for bounded keys. The default for `arr.sort()` in JS is O(n log n) (TimSort), but flagging the assumption is the senior move."

• "Reporting `O(n + 5)` or `O(2n)` instead of `O(n)`. Big-O drops constants and lower-order terms — `O(2n + 100) = O(n)`. Reporting the raw expression in an interview is a tell that you've memorized the form, not the meaning."

• "Confusing time with space. An algorithm can be O(n) time but O(n²) space (e.g. building a distance matrix), or O(n) time AND O(1) space (sliding window). Always name both."
sections.why: The 'inner-loop-not-actually-bounded-by-n' point is the one most worth flagging — it's where candidates get O(n²) wrong in BOTH directions (claiming O(n²) when it's O(n), or claiming O(n) when nested-over-i means it's actually O(n²)). Calling the bound out explicitly — 'inner runs O(n) per outer iteration, so n·n = n²' — is the structural argument the interviewer wants to hear.

sections.title: 3. Spot the math — the recognition checklist
sections.say:
"My read-off-the-shape table:"

• "No loop, no recursion → O(1). Bracket access, hash lookup, arithmetic — work independent of input size."

• "Loop that HALVES the problem each step (`n = n/2`, or binary-search `l..r` shrinks by half) → O(log n). After k halvings the size is n/2^k; loop ends when 2^k ≥ n, so k ≈ log₂(n)."

• "Single loop, one O(1) operation per element → O(n). Sum, max, hash-map first pass, single-pass two-pointer."

• "Sort step + single pass → O(n log n). The sort dominates; addition rule says we keep the largest term."

• "Two nested loops, BOTH bounded by n → O(n²). Even if the inner shrinks (`j = i+1..n`), the sum 1+2+...+n = n(n-1)/2 ≈ n²/2 is still O(n²) after dropping constants."

• "Recursion that splits the input in half AND does O(n) work per level → O(n log n) (merge sort). Recursion that branches twice per call with O(1) work → O(2ⁿ) (naive fib)."

"Then the two arithmetic rules: ADD sequential costs and KEEP the largest term; MULTIPLY nested costs."
sections.why: Having a tight mental table is what lets you answer complexity questions fast — you read the code, match against the shape list, and apply the addition/multiplication rules. The shape-matching skill is also what lets you ESTIMATE complexity for problems you've never seen: the interviewer doesn't care about the answer in the abstract, they care that you have a procedure for arriving at it.

sections.title: 4. Walk through examples
sections.prompt: Run the recognition checklist on three different code shapes.
sections.intro: "Let me apply the read-off-the-shape rules to a few concrete loops."

examples.input: while (n > 0) { n = Math.floor(n / 2); steps++; }  with n=64
examples.note: Halving loop — the canonical log-n shape. Doubling n adds exactly 1 step.
examples.trace:
n=64  →  step 1: n=32
n=32  →  step 2: n=16
n=16  →  step 3: n=8
n=8   →  step 4: n=4
n=4   →  step 5: n=2
n=2   →  step 6: n=1
n=1   →  step 7: n=0   (loop exits)
7 steps  =  ⌊log₂(64)⌋ + 1  =  6 + 1
This is O(log n) by definition.

examples.input: for i in 0..n: for j in i+1..n: count++  with n=4
examples.note: Triangular inner shape — still O(n²) after dropping constants.
examples.trace:
i=0: j=1,2,3   → 3 inner steps
i=1: j=2,3     → 2 inner steps
i=2: j=3       → 1 inner step
i=3: (none)    → 0 inner steps
Total: 3+2+1+0 = 6 = n(n-1)/2
For n=4: 6.  For n=100: ~5000.  For n=1000: ~500,000.
Leading term ≈ n²/2 → O(n²) after dropping the 1/2 constant.

examples.input: arr.sort() + single for loop  with arr.length = n
examples.trace:
sort step:    O(n log n)  ← TimSort on V8
scan step:    O(n)
Total:        O(n log n) + O(n)
Largest term: O(n log n)  ← keep
Drop O(n):    O(n log n)  ✓

sections.why: Walking through the halving loop on concrete numbers — going 64 → 32 → 16 → ... → 0 — is what makes log n feel TANGIBLE. Most candidates can recite 'binary search is log n' but never traced the halvings; once you have, the intuition that 'doubling n adds one step' sticks for life. The triangular-inner trace is the second load-bearing one: it shows WHY a shrinking inner loop is still O(n²).

sections.title: 5. Edges + pitfalls
sections.prompt: Where does naive complexity analysis go wrong?
sections.say:
"Edges where the obvious answer is wrong:"

• "Hash-map ops are O(1) AVERAGE but O(n) worst case (collisions). For interview analysis, ALWAYS state 'average O(1) assuming good hash distribution' — the pathological case requires adversarial input."

• "Amortized analysis. Pushing onto a dynamic array is O(1) amortized: most pushes are O(1), occasional resizes are O(n), but the rare resizes spread out over many cheap pushes average to O(1) per push. Same with Union-Find with path compression — individual op can be O(log n), but n ops total are O(n α(n)) ≈ O(n)."

• "`arr.includes(x)` inside a loop is sneaky O(n²). Each `includes` is O(n); calling it for each element gives n × O(n) = O(n²). Replace with `Set.has` for O(n) total."

• "Recursive Fibonacci `fib(n) = fib(n-1) + fib(n-2)` is O(2ⁿ), NOT O(n). The recursion tree branches twice per call, depth n, so 2ⁿ nodes. Memoization brings it down to O(n)."

• "Space complexity for recursion includes the call stack — depth-n recursion is O(n) space even if it does no allocation. Tail-call optimization isn't reliable in JS, so always count the stack."
sections.why: The `arr.includes` inside a loop case is the most common silent quadratic — it's the bug pattern that gets candidates 'wrong' on a 'right' algorithm. The amortization point is worth raising on any dynamic-array or hash-resize problem; saying 'amortized O(1)' shows you've seen real systems analysis, not just textbook complexity. Stack-as-space-cost is the one most candidates forget on recursive solutions.

sections.title: 6. How I'd justify it in an interview
sections.prompt: Closing the loop — say it out loud, defend the bound.
sections.say:
"My script for stating complexity:"

1. "Name the dominating shape. 'The outer loop is O(n), the inner is O(log n) — so each outer iteration does log n work.'"

2. "Multiply or add. 'Nested → multiply: n × log n = O(n log n). Sequential → add and keep largest: O(n) + O(log n) = O(n).'"

3. "Drop constants and lower-order terms. 'That's O(n log n), not O(2 n log n + 100).'"

4. "State time AND space separately. 'Time O(n log n) from the sort, space O(1) because the sort is in-place — but if I use `[...arr].sort()` instead, space becomes O(n) for the copy.'"

5. "Flag any assumption. 'Assuming hash ops are O(1) average — adversarial keys would make this O(n) per op.'"

"If you want me to extend: the classic interview MOVE is recognizing an O(n²) brute force and replacing it with O(n) via a hash map (Two Sum), or O(n²) → O(n log n) via sort + two-pointer (3Sum). The bound improvement is what the interviewer is grading."
sections.why: The script-it-out approach is what makes complexity claims feel REASONED rather than recited. Saying 'I'm assuming hash ops are O(1) average' is the senior-tier move — it shows you know complexity is conditional on the underlying data structure's guarantees, and you're not blindly applying textbook bounds. Naming the brute-force-to-optimized recognition pattern as the extension proves transfer: this lesson isn't just about reading complexity, it's about USING the recognition to drive optimization.

walkthrough.intro: Step through `countHalvings(n)` — the L3 canonical — to make the log-n shape tangible. Each step halves n and increments the step count. Pick different inputs to see how doubling n adds exactly one iteration.
trace: yield { line: 1, label: `enter countHalvings(${initial}) — expect ≈ log₂(${initial}) + 1 steps`, state: { n, initial } };
yield { line: 2, label: `init steps = 0`, state: { n, steps, initial } };
yield { line: 3, label: `loop check: n=${n} > 0 ✓ — enter body`, state: { n, steps, initial } };
yield { line: 4, label: `halve: n = Math.floor(${prev} / 2) = ${n}  (size ${n === 0 ? 'dropped to 0' : 'now ' + n})`, state: { n, steps, initial, prev } };
yield { line: 5, label: `steps++ → steps=${steps}  (running operation count)`, state: { n, steps, initial } };
yield { line: 3, label: `loop check: n=${n} > 0 ✗ — exit loop`, state: { n, steps, initial } };
yield { line: 7, label: `return steps = ${steps}  (= ⌈log₂(${initial})⌉ + 1 — proof O(log n))`, state: { n, steps, initial, returns: steps } };

notes: Halving each step → log. After k halvings, size is n / 2^k; loop ends when 2^k ≥ n, so k ≈ log₂(n). Doubling n adds ONE step, not double the steps — that's the logarithmic signature.
Drop constants and lower-order terms when reporting Big-O: O(2n + 3) = O(n), O(n log n + n) = O(n log n). The largest term dominates as n grows.

Nested loops aren't always O(n²) IF the inner bound is independent of n — but if the inner bound shrinks predictably (j = i+1…n), the sum is still ~n²/2 → still O(n²). What matters is whether the inner work is proportional to n.
Hash-map operations (`Map.get`, `Map.set`, `Set.has`) are O(1) AVERAGE — assume O(1) for interview analysis. The pathological O(n) only happens on adversarial inputs designed to collide.

questions.q: A loop runs while `n > 0` and does `n = Math.floor(n / 2)` each iteration. What's the complexity in terms of input n?
questions.explain: Halving each step → log. After k halvings, size is n/2^k; loop ends when 2^k ≥ n, so iterations ≈ log₂(n).

questions.q: An algorithm runs in 100 steps when n=1,000 and 200 steps when n=2,000. Most likely complexity?
questions.explain: Doubling n doubled the step count — linear's signature. O(log n) would add ~1 step; O(n²) would quadruple to ~400.

questions.q: An algorithm runs in 100 steps when n=1,000 and ~110 steps when n=2,000. Most likely complexity?
questions.explain: Doubling n added only ~1 step — the unmistakable logarithmic signature. Each doubling of n bumps log₂(n) by exactly 1.

questions.q: Outer `for i in 0..n`, inner `for j in i+1..n`, constant work in the body. What's the complexity?
questions.explain: Inner runs n-i times per outer i. Sum is (n-1) + (n-2) + … + 1 = n(n-1)/2 ≈ n²/2 — still O(n²) after dropping constants.

questions.q: `arr.sort()` followed by one linear scan of `arr`. Total complexity?
questions.explain: Sort is O(n log n), scan is O(n). Sum is O(n log n) + O(n) = O(n log n) by the largest-term rule — the sort dominates.

questions.q: Two loops one after another (not nested): first `for i in 0..n`, THEN a separate `for j in 0..n`. Total time?
options: O(n²) — there are two loops over n
O(n) — sequential loops add (2n), and constants drop
questions.explain: Sequential (not nested) loops ADD: n + n = 2n = O(n). Nesting multiplies; sequencing adds. Only nested-over-the-same-input loops give O(n²).

questions.q: An algorithm builds an n×n distance matrix it must keep around. Its SPACE complexity is:
questions.explain: Time and space are tracked separately — storing n² values means O(n²) extra space regardless of how fast the time is.

questions.q: Pushing n items onto a dynamic array is O(n) total even though an occasional push triggers an O(n) resize. What is this called?
options: Probabilistic O(1) — assumes uniform hash distribution across capacity
Amortized O(1) per push — rare costly resizes spread out over many cheap pushes
Asymptotic O(log n) — the resize threshold doubles each time, so resizes are log n total
Aggregate O(n²) — n pushes can each trigger O(n) work, so the total is O(n²)
questions.explain: Doubling-on-resize makes the expensive operations rare enough that the AVERAGE cost per push is O(1) — that averaged-over-a-sequence cost is the amortized cost.

exercises.prompt: Halving loop: how many iterations until n hits 0? Fill in the termination check.

blanks.hint: stop when n drops to 0 — the final halving of 1 gets you there

exercises.prompt: Nested pair count (the O(n²) shape). Fill in the inner start so each pair is counted once.

blanks.hint: start j one PAST i so you skip self-pairs and duplicates

exercises.prompt: Sort-then-scan (the O(n log n) shape). Fill in the comparator for ascending sort.

blanks.hint: ascending: return negative when a should come before b — so a minus b

L3.prompt: Write `countHalvings(n)` that returns how many times the loop body runs in `while (n > 0) { n = Math.floor(n / 2); }`. Log `countHalvings(64)`.
hints: Initialize a counter at 0 and increment after each halving.
On n=64 you'll see 7 — that's ⌈log₂(64)⌉ + 1 = 6 + 1, because the final halving takes 1 down to 0.
This is the empirical proof of why binary search is O(log n): the step count grows by exactly 1 each time you double n.
